lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and the factory
lead.head: The way station that wasn’t

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 105

body: Is man­u­fac­tur­ing some­thing spe­cial, or is it just like any­thing else? In the sec­ond of two episodes on man­u­fac­tur­ing, Ajay Shah gave his an­swer early: “There’s noth­ing spe­cial about man­u­fac­tur­ing.”

He had been ir­ri­tated by the op­po­site view for thirty years, he said. Development econ­o­mists, in his open­ing words, are “a bit of a creepy bunch”, statist con­trol peo­ple with a “smug com­fort and su­pe­ri­or­ity com­plex that they get to con­trol the world”. {105-J02}
Amit Varma re­ported that be­fore the shoot his co-host had been a vol­cano. On cam­era he was “a flick­er­ing can­dle”, though the light, Varma promised, would still come through.
## How the dogma was built
Shah began with the de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics of the 1960s, 70s and 80s, which rested on four ideas.
Nicholas Kaldor saw that coun­tries with fast GDP growth tended to have fast man­u­fac­tur­ing growth. Wright’s Law, the ex­pe­ri­ence curve, was said to work only in fac­to­ries.

Albert O. Hirschman ar­gued that one fac­tory sparks many oth­ers through link­ages, so the state should get a few going. Hollis Chenery’s World Bank data showed suc­cess­ful coun­tries pass­ing through a phase of heavy man­u­fac­tur­ing be­fore be­com­ing ser­vices economies.

Together they hard­ened into dogma. “Every de­vel­op­ment suc­cess will go through this script,” Shah said. “It is seen as a nec­es­sary way sta­tion, and then you can grad­u­ate to other things.” {105-C01}
The trou­ble began, he ar­gued, when econ­o­mists were will­ing to use state power to fake that stage.
## What went wrong
It did not work, for two rea­sons. Hirschman was right about link­ages, Shah said, but they went global: a German car now car­ries Czech seats, Romanian wiring and soft­ware from Pune.
And pick­ing win­ners fails, be­tween firms or be­tween sec­tors. “There is a role for the state, which is to lay foun­da­tions and then be neu­tral,” he said. {105-C05}

Varma in­sisted that the hosts were not against man­u­fac­tur­ing. Their quar­rel was with co­er­cion: a state that de­clares one path to growth and forces the econ­omy down it, leav­ing a poor coun­try poor for longer.

India, Shah said, is “ground zero” where the old the­ory is being de­stroyed. Over ten years its goods ex­ports grew 38 per cent in nom­i­nal dol­lars, while ser­vices ex­ports grew 126 per cent. Fibre-optic ca­bles, he ar­gued, have made ser­vices more trad­able than goods. {105-C08}
## Umpires and ly­chees

The hosts tested the ar­gu­ment on Bombay’s stalled bid to be­come a fi­nan­cial cen­tre, where trust in in­sti­tu­tions mat­ters more than tech­nol­ogy, and on food, where the Netherlands, the size of Haryana, is the world’s third-largest ex­porter.

What the state owes ev­ery­one, Shah said again and again, is peace, easy taxes and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice. “If you will do peace, easy taxes, and a tol­er­a­ble ad­min­is­tra­tion of jus­tice, we’ve got a lot done.”

Why does the old dogma sur­vive? Varma blamed the lag be­tween the world and those who think about it. “The map of the world is al­ways out of date,” he said; in the world of in­tel­lec­tual con­structs, it is “much more out of date than you would oth­er­wise ex­pect”. {105-C14}
Shah’s lessons for young econ­o­mists were two. Be very cau­tious about cor­re­la­tion and causal­ity. And dis­trust any lead­er­ship role for the state in choos­ing society’s path.
Then he rec­om­mended the books of the very man he had spent the episode crit­i­cis­ing. Hirschman, Shah said, was “one of the great peo­ple”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the export-target meeting

body: Soon after Ajay Shah joined the Ministry of Finance, he sat in on the an­nual meet­ing where of­fi­cials set India’s ex­port tar­get. He asked the room an awk­ward ques­tion: who in this room does any ex­port­ing? {105-S01}

Exporting is done by pri­vate peo­ple, he pointed out. The government’s tar­get, he ar­gued, should be the rules it got out of the way so that those peo­ple could ex­port, not a guess at how much they would sell.

Amit Varma wanted to know whether he got a spank­ing. Not quite. The of­fi­cials treated him like a *naadaan baalak*, a naive child, and told him that when he grew up and be­came a real pol­i­cy­maker, he would un­der­stand the im­por­tance of tar­gets. {#baalak}

quote.text: Exporting is done by pri­vate peo­ple. Who are peo­ple in this room to make up a tar­get?

third.head: Ploughing by telemetry

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the tractor as a sensor platform

body: There is no longer a clear line be­tween man­u­fac­tur­ing and ser­vices, Ajay Shah said. {105-C07} Rolls-Royce does not sell en­gines; it bills by the en­gine-hour and han­dles main­te­nance, fi­nance and in­sur­ance.

A John Deere trac­tor down­loads firmware, probes the soil and sends data to a call cen­tre in Hyderabad, which phones the farmer about an in­fes­ta­tion. “The trac­tor is now a sen­sor plat­form,” Shah said. {#sensor}
His men­tor Kirit Parikh ex­plained the rise of ser­vices long ago: “Once you have enough food to eat, you want the best chef to make the food. And that’s ser­vices.”
Amit Varma had a ques­tion of his own: if you are a man who gets turned on by farm ve­hi­cles, what would those ve­hi­cles be called? Shah’s ver­dict: “Brilliant.” {105-J03}

box.title: The man he argued with
box.text: Ajay Shah spent the episode crit­i­cis­ing Albert O. Hirschman’s work on link­ages, then urged ev­ery­one to read his books and his bi­og­ra­phy, Jeremy Adelman’s *Worldly Philosopher*. Hirschman, Shah said, “led the world’s best life”. {105-R02}

sections.label: The old view
sections.head: Four pillars and a dogma
sections.caption: the four pillars of the old dogma
body: Before tear­ing the the­ory down, Ajay Shah built it up. The de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics of the 1960s, 70s and 80s, he said, rested on four pil­lars, and their his­tory mat­ters.

The first was Nicholas Kaldor’s. In the 1950s, Kaldor ob­served that suc­cess­ful coun­tries which got GDP growth tended to get man­u­fac­tur­ing growth. Shah called it “a crude cor­re­la­tion”. {105-J09}

The sec­ond was Wright’s Law, the ex­pe­ri­ence curve: the more you do some­thing, the bet­ter you get. Economists claimed it hap­pened only in man­u­fac­tur­ing. Produce ten raised to eight ball bear­ings, and you have walked a long way down the cost curve.
## Candles and surges

The third was Albert O. Hirschman’s link­ages. One fac­tory buys raw ma­te­ri­als and sets the stage for oth­ers, so the state should get “a cou­ple of these can­dles going” and let cap­i­tal­ist in­cen­tives fill in the rest. Hirschman called it un­bal­anced growth.

The fourth was Hollis Chenery’s struc­tural trans­for­ma­tion. Working with the first high-quality multi-country data at the World Bank, he and his co-authors found suc­cess­ful coun­tries surg­ing to “twenty forty fifty per cent of GDP as man­u­fac­tur­ing” be­fore be­com­ing ser­vices economies. {#surge}

~ Together the four ideas crys­tallised into dogma: agri­cul­ture must de­cline, man­u­fac­tur­ing must rise, and ser­vices are not im­por­tant. Many de­vel­op­ment econ­o­mists then wanted state power to in­duce the stage. That, Shah said, is “cross­ing a huge line”. {105-C01}

quote.text: It is seen as a nec­es­sary way sta­tion, and then you can grad­u­ate to other things.

portraits.credit: London School of Economics, public domain

sections.label: Mugged by reality
sections.head: There is no German car
sections.caption: why linkages went global
body: The the­ory sounded con­vinc­ing, Amit Varma said, but prac­tice did not turn out as its econ­o­mists ex­pected. Ajay Shah gave two rea­sons.

First, Hirschman was “com­pletely right on link­ages, but the link­ages went all over the world”. There is no German car: its seats are made in the Czech Republic, its wiring in Romania and its op­er­at­ing-system soft­ware by KPIT in Pune. {105-C02}

So the cure is to re­move every fric­tion against in­te­grat­ing with the world: pass­ports, visas, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Enforcement Directorate, cross-border pay­ments, and cur­rent and cap­i­tal ac­count re­stric­tions.
## Picking win­ners

Second, pick­ing win­ners does not work. The state should fix what hob­bles man­u­fac­tur­ing and what hob­bles agri­cul­ture, Shah said, but must never rank sec­tors like a cen­tral plan­ner. {105-C05}

Varma added a clar­i­fi­ca­tion: the hosts were not against man­u­fac­tur­ing. Their quar­rel was with a state that uses co­er­cion to favour one path to growth, which “leaves a poor coun­try poorer” for far longer.

~ Subsidies only fake it, Shah ar­gued. Rig the ex­change rate and the most in­com­pe­tent man­u­fac­turer in India looks glob­ally com­pet­i­tive. “If you sub­sidise some­thing, it will grow. But that’s not growth.” {105-C04}

quote.text: Cars are made all over the world and there is no coun­try any­more.

sections.label: The new model
sections.head: Only the high-skilled game
sections.caption: the high-skilled game
body: If the old model is delu­sional, Amit Varma asked, what is the new one? Ajay Shah’s first an­swer: the vast fac­tory full of un­skilled vil­lagers is over.
Modern man­u­fac­tur­ing runs on au­to­ma­tion and cap­i­tal: com­puter nu­mer­i­cally con­trolled lathes, pro­grammed by English speak­ers who read the man­u­als and watch YouTube guides.

It also de­mands dis­ci­pline. “People have to come to work at 9 a.m. and they have to work cor­rectly for eight hours,” Shah said, be­cause hun­dreds share an as­sem­bly line. {#nine} He sees a real prob­lem with young Indian men: a cul­ture of machismo, vi­o­lence, al­co­hol and late nights.
## Goods or ser­vices?
Second, the line be­tween man­u­fac­tur­ing and ser­vices has dis­solved. Rolls-Royce bills by the en­gine-hour, and a John Deere trac­tor re­ports on the soil to a call cen­tre in Hyderabad.

Third, ser­vices are now more trad­able than goods. When Shah was young, his fa­ther told him that hair­cuts are not trad­able while wid­gets are. {#father} Fibre-optic ca­bles changed that: an ex­change in Chicago takes or­ders from the whole world.

~ So India is “ground zero”. Over ten years its goods ex­ports grew 38 per cent in nom­i­nal dol­lars, about half a per cent a year after US in­fla­tion. {#halfpercent} Services ex­ports grew 126 per cent. “This is a mir­a­cle,” Shah said.

quote.text: There is only a high-skilled game that is avail­able, and we have to play that game.

sections.label: The Bombay dream
sections.head: Stadiums don’t make umpires
sections.caption: umpires, not stadiums
body: Ajay Shah’s test case was Bombay’s bid to be­come an in­ter­na­tional fi­nan­cial cen­tre, a dream that began with a ques­tion from Jaswant Singh when he was Finance Minister. {105-S02}

The first stage is al­ready here, he said. Global firms such as JP Morgan em­ploy huge num­bers of English-speaking Indians to sup­port work done in London and New York. Selling a fi­nan­cial prod­uct made in India to the world is far harder.

A buyer of dol­lar-yen fu­tures is ex­posed, for the life of the con­tract, to ev­ery­thing about the sys­tem that stands be­hind it. {105-C09} That is why Percy Mistry told Shah that good tech­nol­ogy was nowhere near enough.
## The um­pire test
Build the world’s best sta­di­ums at Wankhede or Brabourne, Shah said, and the best teams still won’t come if the um­pires are “thora shady”. {105-C10}
The British, he said, or­gan­ised Wimbledon, and for­eign­ers al­ways win at Wimbledon. Britain built the rules of the game and won the world’s trust that its com­mon law will de­liver. {105-J15}

~ Amit Varma called it in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture. Shah added norms: um­pires and judges be­have bet­ter when their friends ask what on earth they were doing, or when re­searchers crit­i­cise their or­ders. Varma hur­ried to say that Indian um­pires are the best um­pires.

quote.text: It’s not the tech­ni­cal char­ac­ter­is­tics of the sta­dium. The um­pires are key.

portraits.caption: Jaswant Singh
portraits.credit: Aby john vannilam at Malayalam Wikipedia, public domain

sections.label: Food
sections.head: Lychees for Tokyo
sections.caption: the Netherlands and its food exports
body: Before lunch, Amit Varma asked for a story about food, and Ajay Shah of­fered a num­ber. The Netherlands, the area of Haryana or Kerala, is the world’s third-largest food ex­porter, at $140 bil­lion a year. {105-C12}

Agriculture, Shah said, is a site of pro­duc­tiv­ity growth like any other: in­door farm­ing, agri­cul­tural ro­bots, ge­netic en­gi­neer­ing, run by highly skilled peo­ple rather than un­skilled peas­ants.
## Paid for com­plex­ity

The world econ­omy pays for com­plex­ity, he ar­gued. Grow wheat “under the be­nign in­flu­ence of the PDS” and you will not be paid much. Transporting ly­chees from Bihar to Tokyo is com­plex, and pri­vate peo­ple, not the gov­ern­ment, worked out that trade. {#lychee}
India is al­ready partly there. Its food ex­ports, about $43 bil­lion, ex­ceed its tex­tile and ap­parel ex­ports of $34 bil­lion. {#food43}
Varma re­called the farmer leader Sharad Joshi’s cou­plet on the APMC mo­nop­o­lies, which squeezed farm­ers and con­sumers at once. {105-S05}

~ The Netherlands re­minded Varma of Iceland, which drew one-all with Argentina at the 2018 World Cup with a pop­u­la­tion, he cal­cu­lated, the size of Versova. “Iceland is three hun­dred thou­sand fish­er­men,” Shah said.

quote.text: Agriculture is only low grade if your imag­i­na­tion is low grade.

Umpires are not made just by law. They’re made by peo­ple. They’re made by re­spect. An um­pire should feel em­bar­rassed when they go home in the evening and their friends say to them, What the hell were you doing?

p3.title: Stories before lunch
p3.deck: A minister’s dream, a payment that ran late and a farmer’s couplet

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a minister’s question and a stalled dream
stories.head: Bombay’s long game against London
body: The idea did not come from the econ­o­mists. When Jaswant Singh was Finance Minister, Ajay Shah re­called, he sat with Rakesh Mohan and Shah and asked whether they had thought about Bombay as a global pro­ducer of fi­nan­cial ser­vices. {105-S02}
“I know this will take twenty-five years,” the min­is­ter said, as Shah tells it, “but you have to play for twenty-five years. And Bombay must chal­lenge London.”

London makes im­mense amounts of GDP as the world’s fi­nan­cial cen­tre. The ques­tion led to a gov­ern­ment com­mit­tee headed by Shah’s friend Percy Mistry, whose re­port, *Bombay as an International Financial Centre*, came out in 2007. {#report}

The raw ma­te­rial, Shah said, was al­ready there. JP Morgan has per­haps 60,000 peo­ple in India. {#jpmorgan} Throw a stone at any res­i­den­tial build­ing in Bombay, he said, and you will hit some de­riv­a­tives trader, while peo­ple in cof­fee shops strike com­plex fi­nan­cial deals.

What was miss­ing was cor­rect fi­nan­cial reg­u­la­tion and a city fit to live in. A great fi­nan­cial cen­tre needs 100,000 ex­pats in the world’s best-paid jobs to re­lo­cate there, and po­lice sta­tions that can deal with them in English. {#expats}
The work led to FSLRC and a draft law. “But then ev­ery­thing got de­railed,” Shah said.
~ Some 25 years after the minister’s ques­tion, he thinks the job has passed on. The next gen­er­a­tion, he said, must pick up the pieces and build a Bombay “that you would like to live in”.
stories.why: One good ques­tion from a min­is­ter can launch a re­form that runs for decades, and it can stall just as eas­ily. The hosts tell how Indian fi­nance got stuck in an ear­lier episode, *The Journey of Indian Finance*. {105-R12}
stories.postscript: Shah, on Bombay’s traders, to Varma: “I know you hang out with the peo­ple who do con­ver­sa­tions about poker.” {105-J04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the dream of Bombay as a financial centre

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the lesson Percy Mistry taught him
stories.head: The microphone and the promise
body: As a young man, Ajay Shah was proud that NSE had the best com­puter tech­nol­ogy in the world, and thought it was ready to serve cus­tomers ev­ery­where. Percy Mistry stopped him: “No, hold on, you need much more.” {105-S03}
Take a mi­cro­phone, Shah said, like the one on the table. Once it is made and tested, no­body cares where it came from.

A fi­nan­cial prod­uct is dif­fer­ent. Hold a two-month dol­lar-yen fu­tures po­si­tion in Chicago and, for those two months, you de­pend on a whole ma­chin­ery of pri­vate in­sti­tu­tions, reg­u­la­tors and law. “Percy said the qual­ity of the fi­nan­cial prod­uct is the qual­ity of its in­sti­tu­tional en­vi­ron­ment.” {105-C09}
~ NSE once had a real edge in tech­nol­ogy, Shah said. Today the West has caught up.
stories.why: Technology is not the moat in fi­nan­cial ser­vices; in­sti­tu­tions are. A fi­nan­cial prod­uct is a prom­ise that lasts over time, and buy­ing it means trust­ing the coun­try that stands be­hind it.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Percy Mistry’s lesson

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the day NSE was late with payments
stories.head: One bad day, twenty-five years
body: In 2019, for­eign par­tic­i­pants on NSE faced a pay­ment delay be­cause of what Ajay Shah called “some stupid dis­pute be­tween NSE and SEBI”. Jayanth R Varma wrote about it on his blog. {105-S04}
Reading it, Shah re­mem­bered Percy Mistry’s les­son all over again. “You can’t have a pay­ment fail­ure at NSE,” he said. “It doesn’t mat­ter why it hap­pened.”
The show must go on, he ar­gued. Under no cir­cum­stances do you delay a pay­ment to a cus­tomer, least of all a for­eign one, and SEBI and NSE need the ca­pa­bil­ity to make sure of it.
~ On that day, the for­eigner de­cides that pay­ments can­not be trusted to come cor­rectly out of an Indian ex­change. Rebuilding that good­will, Shah said, can take twenty-five years. {#goodwill}
stories.why: Trust in fi­nan­cial in­fra­struc­ture takes decades to build and one bad day to lose. Whatever the quar­rel in­side, an in­sti­tu­tion needs the com­pe­tence to keep pay­ing its cus­tomers, and to keep the show going.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the 2019 payment delay

stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls the farmer leader Sharad Joshi
stories.head: Cheap to sell, dear to buy
body: As the talk turned to food, Amit Varma re­called the farmer leader Sharad Joshi, one of the post-independence politi­cians he truly ad­mires, “be­cause he cared about free­dom”. {#joshi}
Joshi took aim at the APMCs. Granted a mo­nop­oly by the state, Varma said, they could buy from the farmer at one rupee and sell to the con­sumer at twenty ru­pees, and nei­ther had a choice.
Joshi summed it up in a *sher*, spo­ken from a farmer to a con­sumer: “Marte hum bhi hain, marte tum bhi ho. Hum sasta bech ke marte hain, tum mehenga kha­reed ke marte ho.” {105-S05}
~ Varma trans­lated: “I die, my friend, and so do you. I sell my pro­duce cheap and die. You pay too much and you die too.”
stories.why: A middleman’s mo­nop­oly granted by the state does not trade the farmer off against the con­sumer. It hurts both at once, and one cou­plet says what pages of pol­icy anal­y­sis argue.
stories.postscript: Varma has made the case him­self in an ar­ti­cle, *The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer*.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 105. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Albert O. Hirschman (Sgt. Charles James, public domain); Nicholas Kaldor (London School of Economics, public domain); Jaswant Singh (Aby john vannilam at Malayalam Wikipedia, public domain).

shelf.title: Worldly Philosopher: The Odyssey of Albert O. Hirschman
shelf.creator: Jeremy Adelman
shelf.why: Hirschman was far more than an econ­o­mist: a thinker and po­lit­i­cal philoso­pher who, in Ajay’s words, ‘led the world’s best life’.

shelf.title: The books of Albert O. Hirschman
shelf.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
shelf.why: Hirschman wasn’t wrong about link­ages; they sim­ply moved be­yond na­tional bor­ders.

shelf.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
shelf.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
shelf.why: Hirschman’s frame­work of exit, voice and loy­alty shows what India un­der­uses: Indians rely on loy­alty or a lit­tle voice, while Americans exit, mov­ing if they dis­like their city or state.

shelf.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Ep 104, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of why Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is weak: eight ways it dif­fers from ser­vices, twelve things that hob­ble it in India (from du­ties on im­ported in­puts to labour laws) and seven items for every state’s growth strat­egy.

shelf.title: A petty money dispute holds market to ransom
shelf.creator: Jayanth R Varma
shelf.why: Ajay calls it a ‘great blog article’ on an episode that shows Percy Mistry’s les­son in prac­tice: a fi­nan­cial cen­tre can never let a pay­ment fail, what­ever the rea­son.

shelf.title: The Power of Moore’s Laws (Ep 87, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Built around Wright’s Law: pro­duc­tiv­ity rises about 20% with each dou­bling of cu­mu­la­tive out­put, so vol­ume drives down costs and tiny fac­to­ries can’t com­pete, in ser­vices as well as man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Ep 54, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Ep 55, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles chal­lenge to India’s op­ti­mism about every new road and air­port: in­fra­struc­ture has di­min­ish­ing re­turns, and big re­cent gains brought no com­pa­ra­ble rise in FDI, man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports or jobs.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price in the econ­omy and should be set by the mar­ket: rig­ging it to make ex­porters look com­pet­i­tive is a trans­fer from the poor, and man­ag­ing it in­vites cur­rency crises.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Ep 18, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

shelf.title: Invisible Infrastructure (Ep 82, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Advanced economies run on an in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture of in­sti­tu­tions and norms that makes ev­ery­thing work smoothly.

shelf.title: Beware of Industrial Policy (Ep 89, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case against the state pick­ing win­ners: in­dus­trial pol­icy in de­vel­op­ing coun­tries has to start from state ca­pa­bil­ity and pub­lic choice the­ory.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Ep 38, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s short piece ar­gu­ing that state over­reach, such as state-backed APMC mo­nop­o­lies that squeeze both farm­ers and con­sumers, is at the root of farmers’ mis­ery.

laughs.text: Amit on Ajay’s cool­ing tem­per be­tween the off-camera rant and the record­ing: ‘Ten min­utes ago, be­fore we started the shoot, he was using words like rage and fury. He was then a vol­cano. He is now a flick­er­ing can­dle. But it doesn’t mat­ter be­cause you will still get the light and in­sight.’

Ajay’s open­ing salvo: ‘Development econ­o­mists are a bit of a creepy bunch. They are statist con­trol peo­ple, and they have long had this smug com­fort and su­pe­ri­or­ity com­plex that they get to con­trol the world.’

Right after Ajay’s lyri­cal riff on John Deere trac­tors as sen­sor plat­forms, Amit tries a groaner pun: ‘If you are a man who gets turned on by farm ve­hi­cles, what would those ve­hi­cles be called?’ Ajay’s ver­dict: ‘Brilliant.’

Ajay’s test for a real fi­nan­cial cen­tre: ‘You throw a stone at any res­i­den­tial build­ing in Bombay, and you will hit some de­riv­a­tives trader.’ He then ribs Amit: ‘I know you hang out with the peo­ple who do con­ver­sa­tions about poker, but I hang out with the peo­ple who do con­ver­sa­tions about de­riv­a­tives trad­ing.’

Amit on the roller coaster of Ajay’s ex­am­ple: being in­vited to imag­ine a thou­sand-crore dol­lar-yen fu­tures po­si­tion felt great, since ‘I have never traded in fu­tures or op­tions, and I have much closer to a thou­sand ru­pees than a thou­sand crores. But much, much closer.’ Then the poker jibe brought him crash­ing down.
Amit’s hasty dis­claimer after the ‘shady umpires’ anal­ogy: ‘When he talks about um­pires, he is not im­ply­ing that Indian um­pires are bad. Indian um­pires are the best um­pires.’

Amit re­veals Ajay’s ‘met­ric for goodness’: the frac­tion of Everything is Everything episodes you’ve watched. ‘At noon every Friday, even if you were hun­dred per­cent good at eleven fifty-nine, you get a lit­tle less good be­cause a new episode is out,’ but watch­ing at 3x speed lets you catch up fast. ‘So my ques­tion for you, dear lis­ten­ers, is: are you good?’
Nicholas Kaldor’s ‘laws of growth’: his 1950s ob­ser­va­tion that man­u­fac­tur­ing growth tracks GDP growth, the first pil­lar of the man­u­fac­tur­ing dogma.
Japan’s MITI: ‘For every one Japanese MITI that did some good things, I can show you 50 other ex­am­ples where in­dus­trial pol­icy went wrong.’
Wimbledon: ‘The British or­ga­nized Wimbledon and for­eign­ers al­ways win at Wimbledon. That’s the glory of Britain,’ cred­ited to rule of law and the world’s trust in British com­mon law.
